rules.title: Permissions on the API server pod specification file are set to 600 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: The kube-apiserver static pod specification file (/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml) defines how the Kubernetes API server is started on the control plane, including arguments, mounts, and certificates.
rules.impact: Excessive permissions allow unauthorized users to alter API server configuration, weakening authentication, authorization, and TLS settings that protect the cluster control plane.
rules.scope: Verify on the control plane node; Command: stat -c %a /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml Ensure that permissions are set to 600 or more restrictive.

rules.title: Ownership of the API server pod specification file is set to root:root
rules.explanation: The kube-apiserver static pod specification file is owned by a specific user and group on the control plane node. Ownership should be root:root so only privileged administrators can modify it.
rules.impact: Non-root ownership enables a compromised account to change API server startup parameters and potentially disable critical security controls.
rules.scope: Verify on a control plane node; Command: stat -c %U:%G /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml Ensure that the owner is set to root:root.

rules.title: Permissions on the controller manager pod specification file are set to 600 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: The kube-controller-manager static pod specification file (/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml) defines how the controller manager runs on the control plane.
rules.impact: Writable access to this file allows attackers to modify controller manager behavior, including service account signing and garbage collection settings that affect cluster integrity.
rules.scope: Control plane node check; Command: stat -c %a /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml Ensure that permissions are set to 600 or more restrictive.

rules.title: Ownership of the controller manager pod specification file is set to root:root
rules.explanation: The kube-controller-manager static pod specification file should be owned by root:root so only system administrators can change its contents.
rules.impact: Incorrect ownership allows non-privileged users to alter controller manager configuration and weaken least-privilege and credential controls.
rules.scope: Verify on the control plane node; Command: stat -c %U:%G /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml Ensure that the owner is set to root:root.

rules.title: Permissions on the scheduler pod specification file are set to 600 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: The kube-scheduler static pod specification file (/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml) controls how the scheduler component is launched on the control plane.
rules.impact: Open permissions allow unauthorized modification of scheduler settings, which can disrupt workload placement or expose insecure scheduler endpoints.
rules.scope: Verify on the control plane node; Command: stat -c %a /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml Ensure that permissions are set to 600 or more restrictive.

rules.title: Ownership of the scheduler pod specification file is set to root:root
rules.explanation: The kube-scheduler static pod specification file should be owned by root:root to limit who can change scheduler startup configuration.
rules.impact: Non-root ownership increases the risk that a lower-privileged process can tamper with scheduler configuration and cluster scheduling behavior.
rules.scope: Verify on a control plane node; Command: stat -c %U:%G /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml Ensure that the owner is set to root:root.

rules.title: Permissions on the etcd pod specification file are set to 600 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: The etcd static pod specification file (/etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml) defines how etcd, the cluster key-value store, is started on the control plane.
rules.impact: Unauthorized changes to this file can weaken etcd TLS, authentication, or data-directory settings and expose the cluster state store.
rules.scope: Verify on a control plane node; Command: stat -c %a /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml Ensure that permissions are set to 600 or more restrictive.

rules.title: Ownership of the etcd pod specification file is set to root:root
rules.explanation: The etcd static pod specification file should be owned by root:root so only administrators can modify etcd startup parameters.
rules.impact: Incorrect ownership allows tampering with etcd configuration, risking disclosure or corruption of cluster state stored in etcd.
rules.scope: Verify on the control plane node; Command: stat -c %U:%G /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml Ensure that the owner is set to root:root.

rules.title: Permissions on Container Network Interface (CNI) files are set to 600 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: CNI configuration files define how pod networking and the cluster overlay network are configured. Their paths depend on the CNI plugin in use.
rules.impact: Writable CNI files allow attackers to alter network configuration, potentially bypassing network controls or redirecting traffic.
rules.scope: Check on the control plane node; Command: stat -c %a <path/to/cni/files> Ensure that permissions are set to 600 or more restrictive.

rules.title: Ownership of Container Network Interface (CNI) files is set to root:root
rules.explanation: CNI configuration files should be owned by root:root so only privileged administrators can change overlay and pod network settings.
rules.impact: Non-root ownership of CNI files increases the risk of unauthorized network reconfiguration and lateral movement within the cluster.
rules.scope: Check on the control plane node; Command: stat -c %U:%G <path/to/cni/files> Ensure that the owner is set to root:root.

rules.title: Permissions on the etcd data directory are set to 700 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: etcd stores Kubernetes cluster state in a data directory (commonly /var/lib/etcd, or the path set by --data-dir). Directory mode 700 limits access to the owning user.
rules.impact: Broader permissions expose sensitive cluster objects—including Secrets—to unauthorized local users on the etcd host.
rules.scope: On the etcd node, identify the data directory (--data-dir); Command: ps -ef | grep etcd Then check the data directory; Command: stat -c %a /var/lib/etcd Ensure that permissions are set to 700 or more restrictive.

rules.title: Ownership of the etcd data directory is set to etcd:etcd
rules.explanation: The etcd data directory should be owned by the etcd user and group (etcd:etcd) so the etcd process can access its store without granting broader access.
rules.impact: Incorrect ownership can either deny etcd access or allow other local accounts to read or modify the cluster state database.
rules.scope: On the etcd node, determine the data directory (--data-dir); Command: ps -ef | grep etcd Then check the data directory; Command: stat -c %U:%G /var/lib/etcd Ensure that the owner is set to etcd:etcd.

rules.title: Permissions on default administrator kubeconfig files are set to 600 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: Files such as /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf (and super-admin.conf on Kubernetes 1.29+) are kubeconfig credentials created for cluster administrators and contain certificates and keys.
rules.impact: Readable or writable admin kubeconfig files allow unauthorized users to obtain highly privileged cluster access.
rules.scope: Verify on the control plane node; Command: stat -c %a /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf For Kubernetes 1.29 and later also run: stat -c %a /etc/kubernetes/super-admin.conf Ensure that permissions are set to 600 or more restrictive.

rules.title: Ownership of default administrator kubeconfig files is set to root:root
rules.explanation: Administrator kubeconfig files (admin.conf and, where present, super-admin.conf) should be owned by root:root to protect privileged credentials.
rules.impact: Non-root ownership increases the chance that privileged certificates and keys are copied or abused by unauthorized accounts.
rules.scope: Check on the control plane node; Command: stat -c %U:%G /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf For Kubernetes 1.29 and later also run: stat -c %a /etc/kubernetes/super-admin.conf Ensure that the owner is set to root:root.

rules.title: Permissions on scheduler.conf are set to 600 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: The /etc/kubernetes/scheduler.conf file is the kubeconfig used by kube-scheduler to authenticate to the API server.
rules.impact: Excessive permissions on this kubeconfig can expose scheduler credentials and enable unauthorized API access under the scheduler identity.
rules.scope: Verification on the control plane node; Command: stat -c %a /etc/kubernetes/scheduler.conf Ensure that permissions are set to 600 or more restrictive.

rules.title: Ownership of scheduler.conf is set to root:root
rules.explanation: The scheduler kubeconfig file should be owned by root:root so only administrators can read or modify scheduler credentials.
rules.impact: Incorrect ownership may allow credential theft or tampering that impersonates the scheduler to the API server.
rules.scope: Check on the control plane node; Command: stat -c %U:%G /etc/kubernetes/scheduler.conf Ensure that the owner is set to root:root.

rules.title: Permissions on controller-manager.conf are set to 600 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: The /etc/kubernetes/controller-manager.conf file is the kubeconfig used by kube-controller-manager to authenticate to the API server.
rules.impact: Open permissions on this file can leak controller manager credentials and enable privileged API operations under that identity.
rules.scope: Audit on the control plane node; Command: stat -c %a /etc/kubernetes/controller-manager.conf Ensure that permissions are set to 600 or more restrictive.

rules.title: Ownership of controller-manager.conf is set to root:root
rules.explanation: The controller manager kubeconfig file should be owned by root:root to protect credentials used by control loops.
rules.impact: Non-root ownership increases the risk of credential misuse and unauthorized changes to controller manager authentication material.
rules.scope: Verification on the control plane node; Command: stat -c %U:%G /etc/kubernetes/controller-manager.conf Ensure that the owner is set to root:root.

rules.title: Ownership of the Kubernetes PKI directory and files is set to root:root
rules.explanation: Kubernetes stores cluster certificates and keys under /etc/kubernetes/pki/. The PKI directory and its contents should be owned by root:root.
rules.impact: Incorrect PKI ownership can allow unauthorized access to certificates and private keys that authenticate control-plane components.
rules.scope: Verification on the control plane node; Command: ls -laR /etc/kubernetes/pki/ Ensure that the owner of all files and directories in the hierarchy is root:root.

rules.title: Permissions on Kubernetes PKI certificate files are set to 600 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: Certificate files under /etc/kubernetes/pki/ (typically *.crt) are used by Kubernetes components for TLS identity and trust.
rules.impact: Overly permissive certificate files increase the risk of unauthorized reading or substitution of trust material used across the control plane.
rules.scope: Check on the control-plane node; Command: stat -c '%a' /etc/kubernetes/pki/*.crt Ensure that permissions are set to 600 or more restrictive. or ls -l /etc/kubernetes/pki/*.crt — ensure -rw-------.

rules.title: Permissions on Kubernetes PKI key files are set to 600
rules.explanation: Private key files under /etc/kubernetes/pki/ (typically *.key) protect the confidentiality of component TLS identities and must not be world- or group-readable.
rules.impact: Exposed private keys enable impersonation of Kubernetes components and complete compromise of encrypted control-plane communications.
rules.scope: Check on the control-plane node; Command: stat -c '%a' /etc/kubernetes/pki/*.key Ensure that permissions are set to 600 or more restrictive. or ls -l /etc/kubernetes/pki/*.key — ensure -rw-------.

rules.title: The API server --anonymous-auth argument is set to false
rules.explanation: The kube-apiserver --anonymous-auth flag controls whether requests that fail other authentication methods are treated as anonymous and still processed by the API server.
rules.impact: Anonymous access expands the attack surface of the API server. Disabling it forces callers to authenticate, reducing unauthorized discovery and unauthenticated request paths.
rules.scope: Check on a control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that the --anonymous-auth argument is set to false. Alternative check: kubectl get pod -nkube-system -lcomponent=kube-apiserver -o=jsonpath='{range.items[]}{.spec.containers[].command} {"\n"}{end}' | grep '--anonymous-auth' | grep -i false If the return code is 1, the control is missing or has failed.

rules.title: The API server --token-auth-file argument is not set
rules.explanation: The --token-auth-file argument enables static token file authentication on the API server. Tokens are stored in plaintext and require an API server restart to rotate or revoke.
rules.impact: Static tokens are difficult to revoke and easy to exfiltrate if the token file is exposed, making them unsuitable for production authentication.
rules.scope: Control plane node check; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that the --token-auth-file argument is absent. Alternative check: kubectl get pod -nkube-system -lcomponent=kube-apiserver -o=jsonpath='{range.items[]}{.spec.containers[].command} {"\n"}{end}' | grep '--token-auth-file' | grep -i false If the return code is 1, the control is absent or failed.

rules.title: The DenyServiceExternalIPs admission controller is enabled
rules.explanation: DenyServiceExternalIPs is an admission controller that rejects new use of the Service.externalIPs field, which can otherwise route traffic to attacker-controlled destinations.
rules.impact: Unrestricted externalIPs usage can enable network interception or redirection. Enabling this admission controller reduces that risk unless a controlled exception policy is required.
rules.scope: Audit on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that DenyServiceExternalIPs is present in --disable-admission-plugins.

rules.title: The API server --kubelet-client-certificate and --kubelet-client-key arguments are set
rules.explanation: These flags provide the client certificate and key the API server uses to authenticate to kubelet HTTPS endpoints when retrieving logs, attaching to pods, or port-forwarding.
rules.impact: Without client authentication, API server-to-kubelet requests are anonymous, increasing the risk of unauthorized kubelet API use if network access is obtained.
rules.scope: Check on a control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that the --kubelet-client-certificate and --kubelet-client-key arguments are set appropriately. Alternative check: kubectl get pod -nkube-system -lcomponent=kube-apiserver -o=jsonpath='{range.items[]}{.spec.containers[].command} {"\n"}{end}' | grep '--kubelet-client-certificate' | grep -i false If the return code is 1, the control is absent or has failed.

rules.title: The API server --kubelet-certificate-authority argument is set
rules.explanation: The --kubelet-certificate-authority flag configures the CA bundle the API server uses to verify kubelet serving certificates before establishing HTTPS connections.
rules.impact: Without kubelet certificate verification, API server-to-kubelet traffic is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks on untrusted networks.
rules.scope: Check on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that the --kubelet-certificate-authority argument is set appropriately. Alternative check: kubectl get pod -nkube-system -lcomponent=kube-apiserver -o=jsonpath='{range.items[]}{.spec.containers[].command} {"\n"}{end}' | grep '--kubelet-certificate-Authority' | grep -i false If the return code is 1, the control is absent or has failed.

rules.title: The API server --authorization-mode argument is not set to AlwaysAllow
rules.explanation: AlwaysAllow authorization mode permits every authenticated (and, depending on configuration, anonymous) request without further authorization checks.
rules.impact: AlwaysAllow disables meaningful authorization and must not be used in production clusters, where RBAC or equivalent controls are required.
rules.scope: Verification on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that the --authorization-mode argument is set and is not AlwaysAllow.

rules.title: The API server --authorization-mode argument includes Node
rules.explanation: Node authorization mode limits kubelets to reading only the Secrets, ConfigMaps, PersistentVolumes, and PersistentVolumeClaims associated with their own nodes.
rules.impact: Without Node authorization, kubelets may obtain broader cluster object access than required, increasing the blast radius of a compromised node.
rules.scope: Check on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that the --authorization-mode argument includes Node.

rules.title: The API server --authorization-mode argument includes RBAC
rules.explanation: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) authorizes API requests based on Roles and ClusterRoles bound to users, groups, and service accounts.
rules.impact: RBAC provides fine-grained least-privilege control over cluster operations. Omitting it leaves authorization coarse or effectively disabled.
rules.scope: Check on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that the --authorization-mode argument includes RBAC.

rules.title: The EventRateLimit admission control plugin is enabled
rules.explanation: EventRateLimit is an admission plugin that limits how many Event objects the API server accepts in a given interval, protecting the control plane from event floods.
rules.impact: Without rate limiting, misbehaving or malicious workloads can overwhelm the API server with events and degrade cluster availability, especially in multi-tenant environments.
rules.scope: Verify on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that --enable-admission-plugins includes EventRateLimit.

rules.title: The AlwaysAdmit admission control plugin is not enabled
rules.explanation: AlwaysAdmit is a deprecated admission plugin that admits all requests without filtering. Its effect is equivalent to running with no admission controllers.
rules.impact: Enabling AlwaysAdmit disables admission policy enforcement and allows insecure or non-compliant objects to enter the cluster unchecked.
rules.scope: Verify on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that --enable-admission-plugins does not include AlwaysAdmit.

rules.title: The AlwaysPullImages admission control plugin is enabled
rules.explanation: AlwaysPullImages forces every new pod to pull its images before containers start, so image use depends on valid registry credentials rather than a locally cached image name.
rules.impact: Without this policy, once an image is present on a node any pod can reuse it by name, undermining private image access controls in multi-tenant clusters.
rules.scope: Verify on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that --enable-admission-plugins includes AlwaysPullImages.

rules.title: The ServiceAccount admission control plugin is enabled
rules.explanation: The ServiceAccount admission plugin automates mounting and management of service account credentials for pods and must not be disabled via --disable-admission-plugins.
rules.impact: Disabling ServiceAccount admission breaks consistent service account token handling and weakens automated credential controls for workloads.
rules.scope: Verification on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that --disable-admission-plugins does not include ServiceAccount.

rules.title: The NamespaceLifecycle admission control plugin is enabled
rules.explanation: NamespaceLifecycle prevents creation of objects in nonexistent namespaces and blocks new objects in namespaces that are terminating.
rules.impact: Without this plugin, objects can be created in invalid or terminating namespaces, undermining namespace isolation and orderly teardown.
rules.scope: Verify on a control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that --disable-admission-plugins does not include NamespaceLifecycle.

rules.title: The NodeRestriction admission control plugin is enabled
rules.explanation: NodeRestriction limits what a kubelet can modify to its own Node object and the Pod objects bound to that node.
rules.impact: Without NodeRestriction, a compromised kubelet could modify unrelated nodes or pods and escalate within the cluster.
rules.scope: Verify on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that --enable-admission-plugins includes NodeRestriction.

rules.title: The API server --profiling argument is set to false
rules.explanation: The kube-apiserver --profiling flag enables the Go pprof profiling endpoints, which expose detailed runtime information about the API server process.
rules.impact: Profiling data can reveal internals useful to an attacker. Disabling profiling when not needed for troubleshooting reduces the control-plane attack surface.
rules.scope: Verify on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that the --profiling argument is set to false.

rules.title: The API server --audit-log-path argument is set
rules.explanation: The --audit-log-path argument enables API server audit logging and specifies where audit events are written.
rules.impact: Without audit logging, administrators lack a chronological record of API activity needed to detect and investigate unauthorized or suspicious cluster operations.
rules.scope: Verify on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that the --audit-log-path argument is set appropriately.

rules.title: The API server --audit-log-maxage argument is set to 30 or an appropriate value
rules.explanation: The --audit-log-maxage argument defines the maximum number of days to retain old audit log files before they are deleted.
rules.impact: Insufficient retention reduces the ability to investigate historical incidents. A value of 30 days, or another value aligned with organizational policy, preserves forensic value.
rules.scope: Audit on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that --audit-log-maxage is set to 30 or another appropriate value.

rules.title: The API server --audit-log-maxbackup argument is set to 10 or an appropriate value
rules.explanation: The --audit-log-maxbackup argument sets how many rotated audit log files the API server retains.
rules.impact: Retaining an adequate number of rotated logs ensures enough historical audit data remains available for correlation and incident response.
rules.scope: Verify on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that --audit-log-maxbackup is set to 10 or another appropriate value.

rules.title: The API server --audit-log-maxsize argument is set to 100 or an appropriate value
rules.explanation: The --audit-log-maxsize argument sets the maximum size in megabytes of an audit log file before rotation occurs.
rules.impact: Appropriate rotation sizing helps retain usable audit history without exhausting disk space on control-plane nodes.
rules.scope: Audit on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that --audit-log-maxsize is set to 100 or another appropriate value.

rules.title: The API server --request-timeout argument is set appropriately
rules.explanation: The --request-timeout argument sets the global timeout for API server requests. The default is 60 seconds and should be changed only when operationally justified.
rules.impact: A timeout that is too low can disrupt legitimate slow clients, while a timeout that is too high can exhaust API server resources and enable denial-of-service conditions.
rules.scope: Audit on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that --request-timeout is not set or is set to an appropriate value.

rules.title: The API server --service-account-lookup argument is set to true
rules.explanation: When --service-account-lookup is true, the API server verifies that a service account referenced by a token still exists in etcd, not only that the token signature is valid.
rules.impact: Without lookup, deleted service account tokens can remain usable, creating a time-of-check versus time-of-use gap that enables stale credential abuse.
rules.scope: Verification on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that if --service-account-lookup is set, it is set to true.

rules.title: The API server --service-account-key-file argument is set
rules.explanation: The --service-account-key-file argument supplies the public key(s) used by the API server to verify service account tokens, separate from the API server TLS serving key.
rules.impact: Using a dedicated key pair enables safer service account token key rotation and avoids tying token verification to the TLS serving private key.
rules.scope: Verify on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that --service-account-key-file is set appropriately.

rules.title: The API server --etcd-certfile and --etcd-keyfile arguments are set
rules.explanation: These flags provide the client certificate and key the API server presents when connecting to etcd over TLS.
rules.impact: Mutual TLS between the API server and etcd ensures only authenticated clients can access the cluster state store.
rules.scope: Verify on a control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that --etcd-certfile and --etcd-keyfile are set appropriately.

rules.title: The API server --tls-cert-file and --tls-private-key-file arguments are set
rules.explanation: These flags configure the TLS serving certificate and private key used by the API server for HTTPS client connections.
rules.impact: TLS protects sensitive API traffic in transit. Serving without properly configured certificates leaves control-plane communications exposed to interception.
rules.scope: Audit on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that --tls-cert-file and --tls-private-key-file are set appropriately.

rules.title: The API server --client-ca-file argument is set
rules.explanation: The --client-ca-file argument configures the certificate authority used to authenticate clients that present certificates to the API server.
rules.impact: Client certificate authentication strengthens API access control by binding requests to certificate identities signed by a trusted CA.
rules.scope: Check on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that --client-ca-file is set appropriately.

rules.title: The API server --etcd-cafile argument is set
rules.explanation: The --etcd-cafile argument provides the CA certificate the API server uses to verify the etcd server certificate during TLS connections.
rules.impact: Without etcd server certificate verification, API server-to-etcd traffic is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks against the cluster state store.
rules.scope: Verify on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that --etcd-cafile is set appropriately.

rules.title: The API server --encryption-provider-config argument is set
rules.explanation: The --encryption-provider-config argument points to an EncryptionConfiguration resource that enables encryption of selected API resources at rest in etcd.
rules.impact: Without encryption at rest, sensitive objects such as Secrets stored in etcd are readable if etcd storage or backups are obtained.
rules.scope: Check on a control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that --encryption-provider-config points to an EncryptionConfig file. Additionally, ensure that EncryptionConfig covers all required resources, especially secrets.

rules.title: Etcd encryption providers are configured appropriately
rules.explanation: When etcd encryption is enabled, the EncryptionConfiguration providers determine which cryptographic backends protect resources at rest. Suitable options typically include aescbc, kms, and secretbox.
rules.impact: Weak or identity providers leave encrypted resources inadequately protected. Strong providers reduce the risk of Secret disclosure from etcd data.
rules.scope: Check on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Obtain the EncryptionConfig file specified in --encryption-provider-config. Ensure that for all required resources the encryption provider is set to aescbc, kms, or secretbox.

rules.title: The API server uses only strong cryptographic ciphers
rules.explanation: The API server --tls-cipher-suites setting restricts which TLS cipher suites are accepted for HTTPS connections to the control plane.
rules.impact: Allowing weak cipher suites reduces confidentiality and integrity of API traffic. Restricting suites to strong options hardens TLS against known weaknesses.
rules.scope: Verification on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that --tls-cipher-suites is set according to the remediation procedure.

rules.title: The controller manager --terminated-pod-gc-threshold argument is set appropriately
rules.explanation: The kube-controller-manager --terminated-pod-gc-threshold argument sets how many terminated pods may accumulate before garbage collection begins. The default of 12500 may be too high for some clusters.
rules.impact: An excessively high threshold can exhaust node or etcd resources with completed pods, degrading performance and availability until garbage collection runs.
rules.scope: Audit on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-controller-manager Ensure that --terminated-pod-gc-threshold is set appropriately.

rules.title: The controller manager --profiling argument is set to false
rules.explanation: The kube-controller-manager --profiling flag enables pprof profiling endpoints that expose detailed runtime information about the controller manager process.
rules.impact: Unnecessary profiling increases the control-plane attack surface by revealing process internals that can aid reconnaissance or exploitation.
rules.scope: Verify on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-controller-manager Ensure that the --profiling argument is set to false.

rules.title: The controller manager --use-service-account-credentials argument is set to true
rules.explanation: When --use-service-account-credentials is true, each controller loop runs with its own service account credentials instead of sharing a single controller manager identity.
rules.impact: Per-controller credentials enable least-privilege RBAC for control loops and reduce the blast radius if one controller identity is compromised.
rules.scope: Verify on a control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-controller-manager Ensure that --use-service-account-credentials is set to true.

rules.title: The controller manager --service-account-private-key-file argument is set
rules.explanation: The --service-account-private-key-file argument supplies the private key the controller manager uses to sign service account tokens.
rules.impact: A dedicated signing key supports controlled rotation of service account tokens and avoids overloading other component keys with signing duties.
rules.scope: Verify on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-controller-manager Ensure that --service-account-private-key-file is set appropriately.

rules.title: The controller manager --root-ca-file argument is set
rules.explanation: The --root-ca-file argument provides a root certificate bundle that the controller manager can inject into pods so workloads can verify the API server serving certificate.
rules.impact: Without a trusted root CA in pods, in-cluster clients may fail to validate API server TLS and become vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks.
rules.scope: Check on the control-plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-controller-manager Ensure that --root-ca-file points to a certificate bundle with the root certificate for the API server serving certificate.

rules.title: The controller manager RotateKubeletServerCertificate argument is set to true
rules.explanation: RotateKubeletServerCertificate enables kubelets that obtain certificates from the API server to request and rotate serving certificates as credentials expire.
rules.impact: Automatic serving certificate rotation reduces downtime from expired certificates and sustains availability of authenticated kubelet HTTPS endpoints.
rules.scope: Audit on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-controller-manager Ensure that the RotateKubeletServerCertificate argument is set and equals true.

rules.title: The controller manager --bind-address argument is set to 127.0.0.1
rules.explanation: The kube-controller-manager --bind-address flag controls which interface exposes the controller manager health and metrics endpoints (historically unauthenticated on port 10252/TCP).
rules.impact: Binding only to localhost prevents remote unauthenticated access to controller manager health and metrics data and reduces the cluster attack surface.
rules.scope: Check on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-controller-manager Ensure that --bind-address is set to 127.0.0.1.

rules.title: The scheduler --profiling argument is set to false
rules.explanation: The kube-scheduler --profiling flag enables pprof profiling endpoints that expose detailed runtime information about the scheduler process.
rules.impact: Disabling unused profiling reduces information disclosure risk and shrinks the control-plane attack surface.
rules.scope: Verify on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-scheduler Ensure that the --profiling argument is set to false.

rules.title: The scheduler --bind-address argument is set to 127.0.0.1
rules.explanation: The kube-scheduler --bind-address flag controls which interface exposes the scheduler health and metrics endpoints (historically unauthenticated on port 10251/TCP).
rules.impact: Binding only to localhost prevents remote unauthenticated access to scheduler endpoints and limits exposure of control-plane service metadata.
rules.scope: Verify on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-scheduler Ensure that --bind-address is set to 127.0.0.1.

rules.title: The API server --anonymous-auth argument is set to false
rules.explanation: The kube-apiserver --anonymous-auth flag controls whether unauthenticated requests that are not rejected by other methods are accepted as anonymous.
rules.impact: Disabling anonymous authentication reduces unauthenticated access paths to the API server and encourages reliance on explicit authentication controls.
rules.scope: Check on a control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that the --anonymous-auth argument is set to false. Alternative check: kubectl get pod -nkube-system -lcomponent=kube-apiserver -o=jsonpath='{range.items[]}{.spec.containers[].command} {"\n"}{end}' | grep '--anonymous-auth' | grep -i false If the return code is 1, the control is missing or has failed.

rules.title: The API server --token-auth-file argument is not set
rules.explanation: Static token file authentication stores bearer tokens in plaintext on the API server host and cannot revoke individual tokens without restarting the API server.
rules.impact: Static tokens create long-lived, hard-to-revoke credentials. Removing --token-auth-file eliminates this weaker authentication path.
rules.scope: Control plane node check; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that the --token-auth-file argument is absent. Alternative check: kubectl get pod -nkube-system -lcomponent=kube-apiserver -o=jsonpath='{range.items[]}{.spec.containers[].command} {"\n"}{end}' | grep '--token-auth-file' | grep -i false If the return code is 1, the control is absent or failed.

rules.title: The DenyServiceExternalIPs admission controller is enabled
rules.explanation: DenyServiceExternalIPs rejects Services that specify externalIPs, a field rarely required and commonly abused for traffic redirection.
rules.impact: Enabling this admission controller prevents unauthorized external IP routing unless an organization intentionally allows it under separate policy.
rules.scope: Audit on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that DenyServiceExternalIPs is present in --disable-admission-plugins.

rules.title: The API server --kubelet-client-certificate and --kubelet-client-key arguments are set
rules.explanation: These arguments configure the client credentials the API server presents when connecting to kubelet HTTPS endpoints.
rules.impact: Certificate-based authentication prevents anonymous API server-to-kubelet access and strengthens trust for log, exec, and port-forward operations.
rules.scope: Check on a control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that the --kubelet-client-certificate and --kubelet-client-key arguments are set appropriately. Alternative check: kubectl get pod -nkube-system -lcomponent=kube-apiserver -o=jsonpath='{range.items[]}{.spec.containers[].command} {"\n"}{end}' | grep '--kubelet-client-certificate' | grep -i false If the return code is 1, the control is absent or has failed.

rules.title: The API server --kubelet-certificate-authority argument is set
rules.explanation: This argument configures verification of kubelet serving certificates for API server connections used for logs, attach, and port-forward.
rules.impact: Verifying kubelet certificates mitigates man-in-the-middle risk on the path between the API server and node kubelets.
rules.scope: Check on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that the --kubelet-certificate-authority argument is set appropriately. Alternative check: kubectl get pod -nkube-system -lcomponent=kube-apiserver -o=jsonpath='{range.items[]}{.spec.containers[].command} {"\n"}{end}' | grep '--kubelet-certificate-Authority' | grep -i false If the return code is 1, the control is absent or has failed.

rules.title: The API server --authorization-mode argument is not set to AlwaysAllow
rules.explanation: AlwaysAllow authorization grants every request without evaluating Roles, ClusterRoles, or other authorization modes.
rules.impact: This mode removes authorization enforcement and is unsafe for any production Kubernetes cluster.
rules.scope: Verification on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that the --authorization-mode argument is set and is not AlwaysAllow.

rules.title: The API server --authorization-mode argument includes Node
rules.explanation: Including Node in --authorization-mode applies the node authorizer so kubelets receive only the object access required for their own node.
rules.impact: Node authorization limits lateral movement from a compromised kubelet by preventing broad reads of unrelated Secrets and volume objects.
rules.scope: Check on the control plane node; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that the --authorization-mode argument includes Node.

rules.title: Client certificate authentication is not used for end users
rules.explanation: Kubernetes can authenticate users with client certificates, but those certificates lack a practical revocation mechanism when users leave or credentials are compromised. Component-to-component client certificates remain required and cannot be fully disabled.
rules.impact: Without revocation, compromised or obsolete user client certificates can provide lasting cluster access. Prefer identity providers that support credential revocation for human users.
rules.scope: Review user access to the cluster and ensure that Kubernetes client certificates are not used for user authentication.

rules.title: Service account token authentication is not used for end users
rules.explanation: Service account tokens are intended for in-cluster workloads authenticating to the API server. They are not designed as end-user credentials and historically lack strong revocation and expiration controls; bound token volumes improve expiration but still do not provide targeted revocation.
rules.impact: Using service account tokens for people creates weakly managed credentials that are hard to revoke, increasing persistent unauthorized access risk.
rules.scope: Review user access to the cluster and ensure that a service account token is not used for user authentication.

rules.title: Bootstrap token authentication is not used for end users
rules.explanation: Bootstrap tokens are short-lived credentials intended for joining new nodes to the cluster, not for general end-user authentication.
rules.impact: Bootstrap tokens impose constrained identity naming, do not support MFA, and are a weak general authentication mechanism if used by humans.
rules.scope: Review user access to the cluster and ensure that bootstrap tokens are not used for user authentication.

rules.title: A minimal audit policy is configured
rules.explanation: API server auditing is activated by pointing --audit-policy-file at a policy that defines which request stages and resources are logged.
rules.impact: Without an audit policy, security-relevant API activity is not recorded, weakening detection and investigation of unauthorized access.
rules.scope: Check on one of the master cluster nodes; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver Ensure that --audit-policy-file is set. Check the file contents and ensure that the audit policy is correct.

rules.title: The audit policy covers key security concerns
rules.explanation: An effective Kubernetes audit policy records access to and modification of sensitive resources such as Secrets, ConfigMaps, RoleBindings, and authentication-related objects.
rules.impact: Incomplete audit coverage leaves gaps where privilege escalation or secret access may occur without useful forensic evidence.
rules.scope: Review the cluster audit policy and ensure that it covers at least the following areas: • Access to secrets managed by the cluster. Care should be taken to log metadata only for requests to Secrets, ConfigMaps, and TokenReviews to avoid the risk of logging sensitive data. • Modification of pods and deployment objects. • Use of pods/exec, pods/portforward, pods/proxy, and services/proxy. For most requests, the recommended minimum is metadata-level logging (the most basic logging level).

rules.title: Permissions on the kubelet service file are set to 600 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: The kubelet service unit file (for example under systemd) defines how the kubelet process is started on a worker or control-plane node.
rules.impact: Writable service files allow unauthorized changes to kubelet startup arguments and security-related configuration.
rules.scope: To manage the audit, set the kubelet_service_config variable using the kubelet service file, for example: Export kubelet_service_config=/etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/kubeadm.conf. Manual check: Verify on each worker node; Command: stat -c %a /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf Ensure that permissions are set to 600 or more restrictive.

rules.title: Ownership of the kubelet service file is set to root:root
rules.explanation: The kubelet service file should be owned by root:root so only administrators can modify the kubelet unit configuration.
rules.impact: Non-root ownership increases the risk that a local account can alter kubelet behavior and node security posture.
rules.scope: To manage the audit, set the kubelet_service_config variable using the kubelet service file, for example: Export kubelet_service_config=/etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/kubeadm.conf. Manual check: Verify on each worker node; Command: stat -c %U:%G /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf Ensure that the owner is set to root:root.

rules.title: Permissions on the kube-proxy kubeconfig file are set to 600 or more restrictive if present
rules.explanation: When kube-proxy uses a kubeconfig file, that file holds credentials and cluster connection settings for the proxy. If kube-proxy is configured via a ConfigMap instead, no local kubeconfig file may exist.
rules.impact: Excessive permissions on a proxy kubeconfig can expose credentials that allow unauthorized API access under the kube-proxy identity.
rules.scope: Identify the kubeconfig file used by kube-proxy; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-proxy If kube-proxy is running, determine the kubeconfig location from the --kubeconfig parameter. Audit: Audit on each worker node; Command: stat -c %a <path><filename> Ensure that the file is specified, exists, and has permissions of 600 or more restrictive.

rules.title: Ownership of the kube-proxy kubeconfig file is set to root:root if present
rules.explanation: When kube-proxy uses a local kubeconfig file, that file should be owned by root:root to protect proxy credentials and configuration.
rules.impact: Incorrect ownership can allow credential theft or tampering that affects kube-proxy authentication to the API server.
rules.scope: Identify the kubeconfig file used by kube-proxy; Command: ps -ef | grep kube-proxy If kube-proxy is running, determine the kubeconfig location from the --kubeconfig parameter. Verification: Check on each worker node; Command: stat -c %U:%G <path><filename> Ensure that the owner is set to root:root.

rules.title: Permissions on the kubelet kubeconfig file are set to 600 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: The kubelet kubeconfig file (commonly kubelet.conf, referenced by --kubeconfig) authenticates the node to the API server and defines node identity parameters.
rules.impact: Readable or writable kubelet kubeconfig files can expose node credentials and enable unauthorized API operations as the node identity.
rules.scope: To manage auditing, set the kubelet_config variable to the path of kubelet.conf, for example: Export kubelet_config=/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf. Manual check: Verify on each worker node; Command: stat -c %a /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf Ensure that the owner is set to root:root. Ensure that permissions are set to 600 or more restrictive.

rules.title: Ownership of the kubelet kubeconfig file is set to root:root
rules.explanation: The kubelet kubeconfig file should be owned by root:root so only administrators can access node credentials.
rules.impact: Non-root ownership increases the likelihood of node credential theft and impersonation of the kubelet to the API server.
rules.scope: For audit management, set the kubelet_config variable to the path of kubelet.conf, for example: Export kubelet_config=/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf. Manual verification: Check on each worker node; Command: stat -c %U:%G /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf Ensure that the owner is set to root:root.

rules.title: Permissions on the kubelet client CA file are set to 600 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: The file referenced by the kubelet --client-ca-file argument contains certificate authorities used to authenticate clients connecting to the kubelet HTTPS endpoint.
rules.impact: Tampering with the client CA file can weaken or redirect kubelet client authentication and enable unauthorized kubelet API access.
rules.scope: Command: ps -ef | grep kubelet Find the file specified by the --client-ca-file argument. Command: stat -c %a <filename> Ensure that permissions are set to 644 or more restrictive.

rules.title: Ownership of the kubelet client CA file is set to root:root
rules.explanation: The kubelet client CA file should be owned by root:root to protect the trust anchors used for kubelet client authentication.
rules.impact: Incorrect ownership may allow substitution of a malicious CA and unauthorized authenticated access to the kubelet API.
rules.scope: Command: ps -ef | grep kubelet Find the file specified by the --client-ca-file argument. Command: stat -c %U:%G <filename> Ensure that the owner is set to root:root.

rules.title: Permissions on the kubelet config.yaml file are set to 600 or more restrictive if used
rules.explanation: When kubelet is started with --config, the referenced configuration file (often config.yaml) supplies kubelet settings including security-related options.
rules.impact: Writable kubelet configuration allows attackers to disable authentication, authorization, or TLS protections on the node agent.
rules.scope: To manage auditing, set the kubelet_config_yaml variable using the kubelet config.yaml, for example: Export kubelet_config_yaml=/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml. Manual verification: Verify on each worker node; Command: stat -c %a /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml Ensure that permissions are set to 600 or more restrictive.

rules.title: Ownership of the kubelet config.yaml file is set to root:root if used
rules.explanation: If kubelet uses a --config file, that file should be owned by root:root so only administrators can change kubelet security settings.
rules.impact: Non-root ownership increases the risk of unauthorized changes to kubelet authentication, authorization, and TLS configuration.
rules.scope: To manage auditing, set the kubelet_config_yaml variable using the kubelet config.yaml, for example: Export kubelet_config_yaml=/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml. Manual verification: Verify on each worker node; Command: stat -c %aU %G /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml ```Verify that the ownership is set to `root:root`.

rules.title: The kubelet --anonymous-auth argument is set to false
rules.explanation: The kubelet --anonymous-auth setting (or authentication.anonymous.enabled in the kubelet config file) controls whether unauthenticated requests are accepted anonymously by the kubelet API.
rules.impact: Anonymous kubelet access can expose sensitive node and pod operations. Disabling it requires callers to authenticate before the kubelet serves requests.
rules.scope: When using a kubelet configuration file, ensure that authentication.anonymous.enabled=false. Verify on each node; Command: ps -ef | grep kubelet Ensure that the --anonymous-auth argument is set to false. The argument may be omitted if the corresponding value is set to false in the kubelet configuration file.

rules.title: The kubelet --authorization-mode argument is not set to AlwaysAllow
rules.explanation: Kubelet authorization mode AlwaysAllow permits authenticated requests without fine-grained authorization checks against the API server’s expectations for kubelet access.
rules.impact: AlwaysAllow weakens kubelet access control and can allow broader use of kubelet APIs than intended on each node.
rules.scope: Check on each node; Command: ps -ef | grep kubelet If the --authorization-mode argument is present check that it is not set to AlwaysAllow. If it is not present check that there is a Kubelet config file specified by --config, and that file sets authorization: mode to something other than AlwaysAllow. You can also inspect the current kubelet configuration via the /configz endpoint on the kubelet API port (typically 10250/TCP) with appropriate credentials.

rules.title: The kubelet --client-ca-file argument is set
rules.explanation: The kubelet --client-ca-file argument enables certificate-based authentication of clients (including the API server) connecting to the kubelet HTTPS endpoint.
rules.impact: Without client certificate authentication, kubelet endpoints are more easily abused for unauthorized log access, exec, or port-forward style operations.
rules.scope: Verify on each node; Command: ps -ef | grep kubelet Ensure that --client-ca-file points to the client certificate CA file. If the --client-ca-file argument is absent, check the kubelet configuration file (--config) and ensure that authentication.x509.clientCAFile points to the client certificate CA file.

rules.title: The kubelet --read-only-port argument is set to 0
rules.explanation: The kubelet read-only port historically exposed an unauthenticated API for limited read access. Setting --read-only-port to 0 disables that endpoint.
rules.impact: An open read-only port can disclose sensitive cluster and workload information to unauthenticated local or network clients.
rules.scope: Verify on each node; Command: ps -ef | grep kubelet Ensure that --read-only-port is set and equal to 0. If the --read-only-port argument is absent, check the kubelet configuration file (--config) and ensure that readOnlyPort is 0.

rules.title: The kubelet --streaming-connection-idle-timeout argument is not set to 0
rules.explanation: The --streaming-connection-idle-timeout argument defines how long idle streaming connections (such as exec or port-forward) may remain open. A value of 0 disables the timeout.
rules.impact: Disabling idle timeouts increases risk of resource exhaustion, lingering sessions, and denial-of-service through long-lived streaming connections.
rules.scope: Check on each node; Command: ps -ef | grep kubelet Ensure that --streaming-connection-idle-timeout is not equal to 0. If the argument is absent and a kubelet configuration file is specified (--config), ensure that streamingConnectionIdleTimeout is not equal to 0.

rules.title: The kubelet --make-iptables-util-chains argument is set to true
rules.explanation: When enabled, kubelet automatically manages iptables utility chains required for pod networking so host firewall rules stay aligned with pod network configuration.
rules.impact: Preventing kubelet from managing these chains can leave iptables rules too open or too restrictive, disrupting isolation or breaking required pod connectivity.
rules.scope: Verify on each node; Command: ps -ef | grep kubelet Ensure that if --make-iptables-util-chains is set, it is equal to true. If the --make-iptables-util-chains argument is absent and a kubelet configuration file (--config) is specified, ensure that makeIPTablesUtilChains is not equal to false.

rules.title: The kubelet --hostname-override argument is not set
rules.explanation: The --hostname-override argument replaces the node’s detected hostname in cluster registration and related identity handling.
rules.impact: Overriding hostnames can interfere with TLS name matching and make correlating security logs to physical or virtual nodes more difficult.
rules.scope: Check on each node; Command: ps -ef | grep kubelet Ensure that the --hostname-override argument is absent. Note: this parameter cannot be set via the kubelet configuration file.

rules.title: The kubelet eventRecordQPS argument is set to provide appropriate event capture
rules.explanation: eventRecordQPS rate-limits how many events the kubelet generates per second. A value that is too low drops useful events; 0 removes the limit and may overload the kubelet.
rules.impact: Proper event capture supports monitoring and incident analysis, while unbounded event generation can create denial-of-service conditions on the node.
rules.scope: Audit on each node; Command: sudo grep "eventRecordQPS" /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10- kubeadm.conf Review the value set for the argument and determine whether this has been set to an appropriate level for the cluster. If the argument is absent, check the kubelet configuration file (--config) and the value in it.

rules.title: The kubelet --tls-cert-file and --tls-private-key-file arguments are set
rules.explanation: These arguments configure the TLS serving certificate and private key for the kubelet HTTPS endpoint used by the API server for logs, attach, and port-forward.
rules.impact: Proper kubelet TLS credentials enable encrypted, authenticatable node endpoints and reduce man-in-the-middle risk on API server-to-kubelet connections.
rules.scope: Verify on each node; Command: ps -ef | grep kubelet Ensure that --tls-cert-file and --tls-private-key-file are set appropriately. If the arguments are absent, check the kubelet configuration file (--config) and ensure that tlsCertFile and tlsPrivateKeyFile are set.

rules.title: The kubelet --rotate-certificates argument is not set to false
rules.explanation: The --rotate-certificates setting (with RotateKubeletClientCertificate) allows kubelet to create CSRs and rotate client certificates as they expire when certificates are issued by the cluster.
rules.impact: Automatic client certificate rotation reduces outages from expired credentials and sustains authenticated kubelet-to-API-server communication.
rules.scope: Verify on each node; Command: ps -ef | grep kubelet Ensure that --rotate-certificates is absent or set to true. If the --rotate-certificates argument is absent, check the kubelet configuration file (--config) and ensure that rotateCertificates is not set to false.

rules.title: The kubelet RotateKubeletServerCertificate argument is set to true
rules.explanation: RotateKubeletServerCertificate causes kubelet to request and rotate serving certificates after client credential bootstrap when certificates are obtained from the API server.
rules.impact: Serving certificate rotation prevents downtime from expired kubelet HTTPS certificates and maintains availability of authenticated node endpoints.
rules.scope: Skip this check if serverTLSBootstrap=true in the kubelet configuration or the --rotate-server-certificates parameter is set. Check on each node; Command: ps -ef | grep kubelet Ensure that the RotateKubeletServerCertificate argument is set and equal to true.

rules.title: The kubelet uses only strong cryptographic ciphers
rules.explanation: Kubelet TLS cipher suite configuration restricts which algorithms are accepted for HTTPS connections to the kubelet API.
rules.impact: Weak cipher suites reduce protection for kubelet traffic. Limiting suites to strong options hardens node agent communications.
rules.scope: Cipher suites considered secure: • TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 • TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 • TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305 • TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 • TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305 • TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 • TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 • TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 Verify on each node; Command: ps -ef | grep kubelet If --tls-cipher-suites is set, ensure that it contains only values from the specified set. If the argument is absent, check the kubelet configuration file (--config) and the TLSCipherSuites parameter.

rules.title: A limit is set for pod PIDs
rules.explanation: Kubelet can limit the number of process IDs a pod may create via --pod-max-pids or the PodPidsLimit configuration setting.
rules.impact: Unlimited PIDs allow a single pod to exhaust node process resources and cause denial of service against other workloads on the node.
rules.scope: Check the kubelet startup parameters (--pod-max-pids) and the kubelet configuration file (PodPidsLimit). If neither value is set, no limit is in place.

rules.title: The kube-proxy metrics service is bound to localhost
rules.explanation: kube-proxy exposes metrics and configuration endpoints (such as /metrics and /configz) that can be bound via --metrics-bind-address.
rules.impact: These endpoints typically lack encryption and authentication. Binding them to non-loopback addresses exposes operational data on untrusted networks.
rules.scope: Check the flag and start kube-proxy; Command: ps -ef | grep -i kube-proxy Ensure that --metrics-bind-address is not set to a value other than 127.0.0.1. From the command output, determine the path from the --config parameter. Check the file and ensure that metricsBindAddress is not set to a value other than 127.0.0.1.

rules.title: The cluster-admin role is used only where required
rules.explanation: The built-in cluster-admin ClusterRole grants unrestricted control over all cluster resources. ClusterRoleBindings or RoleBindings to this role should be exceptional and justified.
rules.impact: Overuse of cluster-admin violates least privilege and turns routine credentials into full-cluster compromise paths if they are abused or leaked.
rules.scope: Obtain a list of subjects with access to the cluster-admin role; Command: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o=custom- columns=NAME:.metadata.name,ROLE:.roleRef.name,SUBJECT:.subjects[*].name Review each listed subject and ensure that cluster-admin privileges are truly required.

rules.title: Minimize access to Secrets
rules.explanation: Kubernetes Secrets store sensitive data such as credentials and service account tokens in the API. get, list, and watch permissions on Secrets should be limited to the smallest necessary audience.
rules.impact: Unauthorized Secret access can expose credentials for the cluster and for external systems, enabling privilege escalation and lateral movement.
rules.scope: Audit users with permissions to get, list, or view object secrets in the Kubernetes API.

rules.title: Minimize use of wildcards in Roles and ClusterRoles
rules.explanation: RBAC Roles and ClusterRoles may use "*" to match all resources or verbs. Wildcards can unintentionally grant access to newly added API resources, including CRDs.
rules.impact: Broad wildcards undermine least privilege by granting excessive permissions that expand as the cluster API surface grows.
rules.scope: Obtain roles in all namespaces and check for wildcards; Command: kubectl get roles --all-namespaces -o yaml Obtain cluster roles and check for wildcards; Command: kubectl get clusterroles -o yaml

rules.title: Minimize access to create pods
rules.explanation: Permission to create pods can enable privilege escalation through privileged service accounts, hostPath mounts, or other sensitive pod settings unless constrained by admission policy.
rules.impact: Unrestricted pod creation rights increase the chance that a user can launch workloads that escape intended isolation or obtain elevated access.
rules.scope: Review users with permission to create object modules in the Kubernetes API.

rules.title: Default service accounts are not actively used
rules.explanation: Each namespace has a default service account automatically associated with pods that do not specify another account. Workloads that need API access should use dedicated service accounts instead.
rules.impact: Active use of default service accounts obscures permission review and often leaves broadly shared credentials available to unintended workloads.
rules.scope: For each namespace, verify the default service account permissions and ensure that no restrictions other than the defaults are applied to it. Also ensure that automountServiceAccountToken: false is set for each default service account.

rules.title: Service account tokens are mounted only where required
rules.explanation: Pods can automatically mount a service account token for API server access. automountServiceAccountToken should be disabled when the workload does not need to call the Kubernetes API.
rules.impact: Unnecessary token mounts give attackers who compromise a pod credentials for API access, expanding privilege-escalation opportunities.
rules.scope: Review pod objects and the service account in the cluster and ensure that automountServiceAccountToken: false is set if API access is not explicitly required.

rules.title: Avoid using the system:masters group
rules.explanation: Membership in system:masters confers unrestricted API access that is hard-coded in the API server and cannot be limited by removing RoleBindings or ClusterRoleBindings.
rules.impact: Combined with non-revocable client certificates, system:masters can create permanent cluster-administrator credentials outside normal RBAC controls.
rules.scope: Review all credentials with cluster access and ensure that the system:masters group is not used.

rules.title: Restrict use of bind, impersonate, and escalate permissions
rules.explanation: The RBAC verbs bind, impersonate, and escalate allow subjects to assume other identities, attach powerful roles, or raise their own permissions beyond those explicitly granted.
rules.impact: These permissions are common privilege-escalation paths to cluster administrator and should be granted only when strictly necessary.
rules.scope: Review users who have access to cluster roles or roles with impersonate, bind, or escalate privileges.

rules.title: Minimize access to create PersistentVolumes
rules.explanation: Creating PersistentVolumes can enable HostPath-based access to node filesystems. PersistentVolumes are not constrained by Pod Security Admission in the same way as pods.
rules.impact: Users who can create PersistentVolumes may read sensitive host files even when restrictive pod security policies are enforced, enabling privilege escalation.
rules.scope: Review users with permission to create PersistentVolume objects in the Kubernetes API.

rules.title: Minimize access to the nodes/proxy subresource
rules.explanation: Access to the nodes/proxy subresource grants broad use of the kubelet API, including command execution in containers on the node, while bypassing API server audit logging of those kubelet calls.
rules.impact: nodes/proxy permissions enable privilege escalation and circumvention of cluster audit and access controls and should be tightly restricted.
rules.scope: Review users who have access to the nodes/proxy subresource in the Kubernetes API.

rules.title: Minimize access to the certificatesigningrequests approval subresource
rules.explanation: Users who can update the approval subresource of CertificateSigningRequest objects can approve new client certificates for API access.
rules.impact: CSR approval rights can create highly privileged identities and escalate a user to cluster administrator depending on signer and binding configuration.
rules.scope: Review users who have access to the updated subresource for approving certificate signing request objects in the Kubernetes API.

rules.title: Minimize access to webhook configuration objects
rules.explanation: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration and MutatingWebhookConfiguration objects control admission webhooks that can observe and, for mutating webhooks, modify objects admitted to the cluster.
rules.impact: Unrestricted webhook management can enable privilege escalation, data exfiltration, or disruption of cluster admission controls.
rules.scope: Review users who have access to objects by inspecting webhook configurations or by modifying webhook configurations in the Kubernetes API.

rules.title: Minimize access to service account token creation
rules.explanation: Permission to create tokens for serviceaccounts (the token subresource) allows issuance of credentials that can provide long-lived cluster access.
rules.impact: Unrestricted token creation enables persistent privileged access that may survive revocation of the original user account.
rules.scope: Review users with access to create tokens for the serviceaccount object subresource in the Kubernetes API.

rules.title: The cluster has at least one active policy control mechanism
rules.explanation: Clusters should enforce workload restrictions using Pod Security Admission or an equivalent external policy engine that can deny unsafe pod configurations.
rules.impact: Without an active policy mechanism, privileged containers, host mounts, and similar high-risk settings cannot be systematically prevented.
rules.scope: Review the cluster workload and ensure that a security admission controller or an external control system is used.

rules.title: Minimize admission of privileged containers
rules.explanation: A container with securityContext.privileged set to true receives nearly all host capabilities and device access. Policy should deny privileged pods by default.
rules.impact: Privileged containers can perform almost any host action and greatly increase the risk of container escape and node compromise.
rules.scope: Command: get pods -A -o=jsonpath=$'{range.items[*]}{@.metadata.name}: {@..securityContext}\n{end}' It will produce an inventory of all the privileged use on the cluster, if any (please, refer to a sample below). Further grepping can be done to automate each specific violation detection. calico-kube-controllers-57b57c56f-jtmk4: {} << No Elevated Privileges calico-node- c4xv4: {} {"privileged":true} {"privileged":true} {"privileged":true} {"privileged":true} << Violates 5.2.2 dashboard-metrics-scraper-7bc864c59-2m2xw: {"seccompProfile":{"type":"RuntimeDefault"}} {"allowPrivilegeEscalation":false,"readOnlyRootFilesystem":true,"runAsGroup":2001,"ru nAsUser":1001}

rules.title: Minimize admission of containers that share the host PID namespace
rules.explanation: Setting hostPID to true places a container in the host process identifier namespace so it can observe processes outside its own container.
rules.impact: Host PID sharing, especially with ptrace-related capabilities, can enable privilege escalation beyond the container boundary.
rules.scope: List the policy in each namespace and ensure that the policy denies admission of containers using HostPID.

rules.title: Minimize admission of containers that share the host IPC namespace
rules.explanation: Setting hostIPC to true places a container in the host inter-process communication namespace, allowing IPC with processes outside the container.
rules.impact: Host IPC sharing can expose sensitive host or sibling-workload communication channels and should be denied unless explicitly required.
rules.scope: Enumerate the policy in each namespace and ensure that the policy denies admission of containers with host IPC.

rules.title: Minimize admission of containers that share the host network namespace
rules.explanation: Setting hostNetwork to true places a container in the host network namespace, giving access to host interfaces and traffic paths shared with other pods.
rules.impact: Host networking weakens network isolation, can bypass NetworkPolicy controls, and exposes host services to the container.
rules.scope: Enumerate the policy in each namespace and ensure that the policy denies admission of containers with host networking.

rules.title: Minimize admission of containers with allowPrivilegeEscalation
rules.explanation: allowPrivilegeEscalation controls whether a process may gain more privileges than its parent (for example via setuid). Policy should generally require this setting to be false.
rules.impact: Allowing privilege escalation inside containers increases the chance that a compromised process obtains greater rights than intended within the container.
rules.scope: List the policy in each namespace and ensure that the policy denies admission of containers with allowPrivilegeEscalation.

rules.title: Minimize admission of containers that run as root
rules.explanation: Containers can run as any Linux user. Policies such as MustRunAsNonRoot or equivalent controls should prefer non-root UIDs rather than UID 0.
rules.impact: Root containers remain higher value targets for container escape and host compromise even when constrained by the runtime.
rules.scope: List the policy in each namespace and ensure that the policy restricts running root containers via MustRunAsNonRoot or MustRunAs with a UID range that excludes 0.

rules.title: Minimize admission of containers with the NET_RAW capability
rules.explanation: NET_RAW allows creation of raw sockets and is commonly present in default capability sets for some runtimes. Policy should drop or deny this capability unless required.
rules.impact: NET_RAW can be abused for network spoofing and reconnaissance from within a compromised container.
rules.scope: Enumerate the policy in each namespace and ensure that at least one denies admission of containers with the NET_RAW capability.

rules.title: Minimize admission of containers with capabilities beyond the default set
rules.explanation: Containers start with a runtime default capability set. Adding capabilities beyond that set expands the rights available inside the container.
rules.impact: Extra capabilities increase container-escape and host-abuse opportunities and should be granted only through tightly controlled exceptions.
rules.scope: List the policy in each namespace and ensure that the policy does not allow setting permitted capabilities to any value other than an empty array.

rules.title: Minimize admission of containers with assigned capabilities
rules.explanation: Linux capabilities are subsets of traditional root privileges. Many workloads need none; policy can require dropping all capabilities where feasible.
rules.impact: Reducing assigned capabilities enforces least privilege inside containers and shrinks the impact of application compromise.
rules.scope: Recount the policy in each namespace and ensure that at least one requires the capability to be dropped by all containers.

rules.title: Minimize admission of Windows containers that share host processes
rules.explanation: Windows containers with hostProcess set to true can interact directly with the underlying Windows node and obtain privileged host access.
rules.impact: Host-process Windows containers effectively provide privileged node access and should be denied unless a tightly controlled exception is required.
rules.scope: Enumerate the policy in each namespace and ensure that the policy denies admission of host-process containers.

rules.title: Minimize admission of containers that use HostPath volumes
rules.explanation: A hostPath volume mounts a path from the node filesystem into a container. Policy should deny HostPath use by default.
rules.impact: HostPath mounts can expose sensitive host files and directories to workloads, enabling data theft or privilege escalation on the node.
rules.scope: List the policy in each namespace and ensure that the policy denies admission of containers with HostPath volumes.

rules.title: Minimize admission of containers that use HostPorts
rules.explanation: HostPorts bind container ports directly on the node network namespace. Policy should deny hostPort usage unless explicitly required.
rules.impact: HostPorts can bypass NetworkPolicy controls and unexpectedly expose services on the node network interface.
rules.scope: Enumerate the policy in each namespace and ensure that the policy denies admission of containers with a hostPort section.

rules.title: The CNI in use supports NetworkPolicies
rules.explanation: Kubernetes NetworkPolicy objects are enforced by the cluster CNI plugin. Not all CNI plugins implement ingress and egress policy enforcement.
rules.impact: If the CNI lacks NetworkPolicy support, administrators cannot effectively restrict pod-to-pod traffic even when policies are defined.
rules.scope: Review the documentation for the CNI plugin used in the cluster and ensure that it supports ingress and egress network policies.

rules.title: NetworkPolicies are defined for all namespaces
rules.explanation: A NetworkPolicy selects pods and defines allowed ingress and egress. Namespaces without any NetworkPolicy allow unrestricted pod traffic by default.
rules.impact: Missing network segmentation lets a compromised workload freely reach neighboring applications in the same cluster network.
rules.scope: Check NetworkPolicy objects in the cluster; Command: kubectl get networkpolicy --all-namespaces Ensure that at least one network policy is defined for each namespace in the cluster.

rules.title: Prefer Secrets as files over Secrets as environment variables
rules.explanation: Kubernetes can project Secrets into pods as volumes or inject them as environment variables. File-based projection is preferred where practical.
rules.impact: Environment variables are frequently captured in process listings and crash logs, increasing the chance that Secret values are disclosed.
rules.scope: Search for objects that use environment variables from secrets; Command: kubectl get all -o jsonpath='{range.items[?(@..secretKeyRef)]} {.kind} {.metadata.name} {"\n"}{end}' -A

rules.title: Consider using an external secrets store
rules.explanation: External secret managers can store and deliver credentials outside etcd, often with stronger authentication, auditing, encryption, and rotation workflows than native Secrets alone.
rules.impact: Centralized external secret stores can reduce broad Kubernetes Secret sprawl and improve control when the same secrets are used across Kubernetes and non-Kubernetes systems.
rules.scope: Review the organization's secrets management implementation.

rules.title: Configure image provenance using the ImagePolicyWebhook admission controller
rules.explanation: ImagePolicyWebhook allows the API server to consult an external service that accepts or rejects images based on provenance or allowlist policy before pods are admitted.
rules.impact: Enforcing image provenance helps ensure only approved images are deployed, reducing supply-chain and untrusted-image risk.
rules.scope: Review pod definitions in the cluster and ensure that image provenance is configured appropriately.

rules.title: Create administrative boundaries between resources using namespaces
rules.explanation: Namespaces partition cluster resources into logical groups so RBAC and other controls can scope access by team, application, or environment.
rules.impact: Without namespace boundaries, users and workloads more easily affect unrelated resources, increasing the blast radius of errors and malicious activity.
rules.scope: Review namespaces in the cluster; Command: kubectl get namespaces Ensure that these namespaces meet requirements and are managed appropriately.

rules.title: A seccomp profile is set in pod definitions
rules.explanation: Seccomp (secure computing mode) restricts the system calls a containerized process may make. Pod or container securityContext can set a seccomp profile such as RuntimeDefault.
rules.impact: Without seccomp, workloads retain a broader syscall surface. Enabling a default profile limits actions available after container compromise.
rules.scope: Verify the definition module in the cluster. The following changes must be used: SecurityContext: seccompProfile: type: RuntimeDefault.

rules.title: Apply a SecurityContext to pods and containers
rules.explanation: A SecurityContext defines OS-level security settings such as runAsUser, runAsGroup, capabilities, and SELinux options at pod and container scope in the workload manifest.
rules.impact: Explicit security contexts enforce least-privilege runtime settings and reduce the chance that workloads inherit overly permissive defaults.
rules.scope: Review the definition module in the cluster and ensure that the security context is configured appropriately.

rules.title: Do not use the default namespace for workloads
rules.explanation: Objects created without a namespace are placed in the default namespace. Using dedicated namespaces makes RBAC and related controls easier to apply and review.
rules.impact: Concentrating resources in default mixes unrelated workloads and weakens namespace-scoped security boundaries and operational hygiene.
rules.scope: Check objects in the default namespace; Command: kubectl get $( kubectl api-resources --verbs=list --namespaced=true -o name | paste -sd, -) --ignore-not-found -n default The list should contain only system resources, for example the kubernetes service.
